BiblicalUsage: Chamam is plain physical warmth, and Scripture uses it for bodies, fires, and company alike. David in his old age could not get warm, so his servants sought a young woman to lie beside him and give him heat. Elisha lay upon the dead child until the child's flesh waxed warm, and the Teacher in Ecclesiastes says two lying together have heat while one alone cannot get warm. Isaiah turns the same warmth into mockery: the idol-maker burns part of his wood, warms himself by it, and then bows to the rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe warmth in the Bible is nearly always something shared or given, never hoarded. A fire warms the hands that made an idol out of it, yet the same heat raised a dead child when a prophet stretched himself over him. I hold that God made warmth to be passed from one person to another, and the loneliest picture in Scripture is a man who cannot get warm alone.
